set.detail: The Cantabrian and Asturian wars (29-19 BC) completed the conquest of the Iberian peninsula, two centuries after the first Roman landing in 218 BC. The Cantabri and Astures of the north-western mountains, raiding the plains of the Vaccaei, Turmogi and Autrigones, were the last independent peoples of Hispania. Statilius Taurus fought them in 29 BC and Calvisius Sabinus and Sextus Appuleius triumphed in 28-26, but the main effort came in 26-25 BC, when Augustus himself took command with seven or eight legions (I Augusta, II Augusta, IV Macedonica, V Alaudae, VI Victrix, IX Hispana, X Gemina, XX), the largest concentration of the era. From a base at Segisama, three columns advanced into the mountains while a fleet from Aquitania landed on the coast. Augustus fell ill and retired to Tarraco, and his legates Antistius and Furnius won the battle of Vellica, besieged the Cantabri on Mons Vindius, where they starved, and took Aracillum; Publius Carisius took the Asturian stronghold of Lancia. The temple of Janus was closed in 25 BC and Augusta Emerita was founded for veterans. But the mountaineers rose repeatedly, in 24, 22 and 19 BC, enslaved prisoners killed their masters and returned home, and the Roman troops became demoralised; Agrippa finally ended the resistance in 19 BC with brutal measures, killing most men of fighting age, forcing survivors down to the plains and disgracing a legion (I Augusta, which lost its title). Florus and Orosius, drawing on Livy, record mass suicides by poison from yew trees and captives singing as they were crucified. Three legions stayed in the north-west, and the gold mines of Las Médulas and elsewhere were opened under Roman control. The province of Hispania was reorganised into Tarraconensis, Lusitania and Baetica. Modern archaeology has identified Roman camps and siege works at sites such as La Espina del Gallego, El Cincho and Monte Bernorio, but the identification of ancient place names is often uncertain.

The war between Rome and the kingdom of Kush (Meroë), 25-21 BC, was the first major conflict between Rome and a sub-Saharan African state. In 25 BC, when the prefect of Egypt Aelius Gallus had taken part of the garrison on his ill-fated Arabian expedition, a Kushite army of some 30,000, led by the "one-eyed queen" (the Kandake, probably Amanirenas) and her son Akinidad, attacked Syene, Elephantine and Philae, enslaving the inhabitants and throwing down statues of Augustus. The prefect Gaius Petronius counter-attacked in 24 BC with fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 cavalry, defeated the Kushites at Pselchis (Dakka), took Primis (Qasr Ibrim) and advanced to Napata, the old royal capital, which he sacked in 24 or 23 BC, enslaving its people, according to Strabo. He fortified Primis with a garrison of 400 and two years' supplies. When the Kushites besieged it in 22 BC, Petronius relieved it and the Kandake sent envoys; Petronius sent them to Augustus, who received them at Samos in 21/20 BC and granted all their requests, including the remission of tribute that Petronius had imposed. The frontier was fixed at Hiera Sykaminos (Maharraqa), with the Dodecaschoenus as a Roman buffer zone. The famous bronze head of Augustus found at Meroë in 1910, now in the British Museum, was buried beneath the steps of a victory temple, apparently taken in the raid on Syene. Meroitic inscriptions, including a stele of Akinidad and Amanirenas (in the British Museum), may record the war from the Kushite side but cannot yet be fully read. Modern scholars see the peace as a negotiated compromise that reflected Kushite strength and Roman unwillingness to commit forces so far south; Res Gestae 26 nonetheless claims that Roman armies reached Napata. The frontier remained quiet for centuries.

The Alpine wars of Augustus (25-14 BC) subdued the peoples of the Alps, securing the passes between Italy, Gaul and the Danube and preparing for the advance into Germany and Illyricum. The first step was the destruction of the Salassi of the Val d'Aosta in 25 BC by Terentius Varro Murena, who sold 36,000 of them into slavery and founded Augusta Praetoria. In 16 BC Publius Silius Nerva subdued the Camunni and Vennonetes in the central Alps. The decisive campaign came in summer 15 BC: Drusus advanced from Italy through the Adige valley and the Brenner, defeating the Raeti at Tridentum, while Tiberius advanced from Gaul, using boats on Lake Constance against the Vindelici, and won a battle near the source of the Danube on 1 August, the anniversary of the capture of Alexandria. The two armies met in the Alpine foreland, and the region was organised as the province of Raetia, with Augusta Vindelicum (Augsburg) as its later capital; Noricum was incorporated peacefully around the same time. The Maritime Alps were subdued in 14 BC. Horace celebrated the victories in Odes 4.4 and 4.14. The Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie, dedicated in 7-6 BC, lists 45 conquered Alpine peoples in an inscription preserved by Pliny the Elder. Strabo stresses the strategic importance of the conquest, which ended raids on northern Italy and opened routes over the Great St Bernard, Little St Bernard, Brenner and Reschen passes. Dio mentions the deportation of young men of military age from the Raeti. The Cottian kingdom remained a client state under Cottius, who built an arch at Segusio (9-8 BC), until annexed under Nero. Recent archaeology has found traces of the campaign of 15 BC, including a battlefield at Döttenbichl near Oberammergau with Roman arrowheads and catapult bolts, and Roman camps at Dangstetten on the upper Rhine.

The Pannonian war (14-9 BC) brought the lands between the eastern Alps and the Danube under Roman control, linking Italy with the Balkans and creating the province of Illyricum, later divided into Pannonia and Dalmatia. Earlier campaigns by Octavian in 35-33 BC had taken Siscia and subdued the Iapydes. Unrest broke out in 14 BC and Marcus Vinicius and Agrippa intervened, Agrippa's arrival in winter 13/12 BC being enough to halt the rising. After Agrippa's death in 12 BC Tiberius took over the command, campaigning for four years against the Pannonian tribes, especially the Breuci, with the help of the Scordisci; he used harsh methods, selling the young men into slavery and deporting others, and Dio says he took their arms. In 11 BC Illyricum was transferred from the Senate to Augustus because of the war, and the Dalmatians were subdued as well. Tiberius was awarded an ovation in 9 BC (the Senate voted a triumph but Augustus allowed only an ovation) and triumphal ornaments; Augustus claimed in the Res Gestae (30) that he had brought the Pannonian peoples, never reached before, under the empire and extended Illyricum to the Danube. The sources for the war are thin (Dio's brief notices, Velleius, Suetonius and Florus). The conquest was not secure: the levy imposed on the region and heavy tribute provoked the Great Illyrian Revolt of AD 6-9, led by the Breuci and Daesitiates whom Tiberius had subdued. Later Roman colonies and municipalities at Emona, Siscia, Sirmium and Poetovio and the legionary bases at Carnuntum and Poetovio grew out of the conquest. Modern historians (Wilkes, Šašel Kos) emphasise that the war was a series of punitive and pacifying campaigns rather than a single conquest, and that Roman control of the Danube line itself was only established under Tiberius.

The Augustan Germanic wars (12 BC-AD 16) were Rome's attempt to conquer Germany between the Rhine and the Elbe. After the Clades Lolliana (16 BC) and Augustus's stay in Gaul, Drusus campaigned for four seasons (12-9 BC) from bases at Vetera, Novaesium, Mogontiacum and elsewhere, digging a canal to the North Sea, attacking the Sugambri, Bructeri, Chatti, Cherusci and Marcomanni and reaching the Elbe in 9 BC, where he died. Tiberius continued in 8-7 BC, deporting 40,000 Sugambri across the Rhine. Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus crossed the Elbe c. 3-1 BC. After an "immense war" (immensum bellum) from AD 1, Tiberius campaigned in 4-5 to the Weser and Elbe, with a fleet sailing to Jutland, and in 6 prepared an attack on Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom in Bohemia, abandoned because of the Illyrian revolt. The archaeological evidence of camps at Haltern, Oberaden, Anreppen and Hedemünden and the civil town at Waldgirmes, with a gilded equestrian statue of Augustus, shows that the region was being organised as a province with towns and markets. The project collapsed in AD 9, when Arminius destroyed Varus's three legions in the Teutoburg forest. Tiberius restored the Rhine line in 10-12, and Germanicus, with eight legions, campaigned in 14-16 against the Marsi, Chatti, Bructeri and Cherusci, recovering two eagles and winning battles at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian wall, but with heavy losses from storms and ambushes. Tiberius recalled him in 16, saying that the Germans could be left to their internal quarrels, and the Rhine became the frontier. Modern historians debate whether Augustus aimed at the Elbe as a permanent border, whether Germany was already a province before AD 9 (Dio says so), and why the conquest failed: the decentralised Germanic societies, the military effort needed elsewhere, or the shock of AD 9. The consequences shaped European history by leaving Germany outside the empire.
set.debate: Whether Augustus intended to annex Germany to the Elbe and whether a province existed before AD 9.

set.detail: The Great Illyrian Revolt (bellum Batonianum, AD 6-9) was a rising of the Pannonian and Dalmatian peoples against Roman rule, described by Suetonius as the most serious foreign war since the Punic Wars. It broke out in AD 6 when men summoned for auxiliary service for Tiberius's campaign against Maroboduus turned their arms against Rome, led by Bato of the Daesitiates in central Bosnia and by Bato and Pinnes of the Breuci in the Sava valley. The rebels, numbering according to Velleius 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry, many of them trained in Roman service, killed Roman citizens and traders, attacked Sirmium and Salona and raided Macedonia. Rome responded with an enormous mobilisation: Tiberius, Germanicus and the governors of Moesia (Caecina Severus) and Galatia (Plautius Silvanus) brought up ten legions, more than seventy auxiliary cohorts and fourteen alae, plus Thracian cavalry, while Augustus raised freedmen and slaves for the army. The war was fought in difficult terrain with forts, ambushes and famine: the Romans nearly lost a battle at the Volcaean marshes in AD 7, when five legions were surprised. Tiberius preferred a strategy of attrition, devastating the land and wearing down the enemy. In AD 8 the Breucian Bato betrayed Pinnes and was killed by his Daesitiate namesake, and the Breuci surrendered at the river Bathinus. In AD 9 Tiberius and Germanicus reduced the Dalmatian strongholds of Raetinium, Splonum, Seretium and Andetrium; Bato surrendered and was interned at Ravenna. The war cost Rome heavily in money and manpower, and news of victory came days before news of the Varian disaster. Tiberius celebrated his triumph in AD 12. The region was divided into the provinces of Pannonia and Dalmatia, with legions at Poetovio, Siscia, Burnum and Tilurium. Dio is the main source, with Velleius, an eyewitness officer.

The war of Tacfarinas (AD 17-24) was the most serious resistance to Roman rule in North Africa in the early Principate. Tacfarinas, a Numidian of the Musulamii who had served as a Roman auxiliary and deserted, organised the semi-nomadic Musulamii and their neighbours, the Cinithii and the Mauri under Mazippa, into a force with regular infantry and cavalry units on Roman lines and mobile raiding bands. The war was a reaction to Roman expansion into their grazing lands, the building of the road from Ammaedara to Tacapae by the legion III Augusta in AD 14 and the demarcation of land for taxation and settlement. In AD 17 the proconsul Furius Camillus defeated him in a pitched battle and won triumphal ornaments. In 20 he resumed raids and besieged Roman forts; Lucius Apronius decimated a cohort that had fled and won a victory at Thala. In 21-22 Tacfarinas demanded land for his followers and threatened endless war; Tiberius refused to negotiate with a deserter and bandit, and sent Quintus Junius Blaesus, Sejanus's uncle, who used small mobile columns and winter forts, offered amnesty to all except Tacfarinas and captured his brother, earning the last imperatorial acclamation given to a commander outside the imperial family. After IX Hispana was withdrawn, Tacfarinas reappeared in 24, supported by Moors discontented with the rule of Ptolemy of Mauretania. The proconsul Publius Cornelius Dolabella, with Mauretanian help, surprised his camp at Auzea and killed him; his son was captured. Tiberius refused Dolabella the triumphal ornaments out of deference to Sejanus's uncle, Tacitus says. Tacitus's account (Annals 2-4) is the only narrative. Modern historians see the war in terms of conflict over land between pastoralists and the expanding Roman agricultural frontier, and the military lessons were reflected in Caligula's decision in 39 to place the legion of Africa under an imperial legate.
set.debate: Bandit insurgency (Roman view) or a struggle of pastoralists against the agricultural frontier.

set.detail: The Roman conquest of Britain began with the Claudian invasion of 43 and continued for four decades. Aulus Plautius, with four legions and auxiliaries, defeated the Catuvellauni under Caratacus and Togodumnus at the Medway and Thames, and Claudius received the surrender of eleven kings at Camulodunum. Vespasian with II Augusta subdued the south-west, taking Maiden Castle and other hillforts. By 47 the province extended to the line of the Fosse Way. Client kingdoms, Togidubnus of the Regni, Prasutagus of the Iceni and Cartimandua of the Brigantes, protected the flanks. Ostorius Scapula (47-52) disarmed the tribes, crushed the first Iceni revolt and defeated Caratacus in Wales (51), who was handed over by Cartimandua; the Silures continued the struggle. Didius Gallus and Veranius held the line, and Suetonius Paullinus attacked the Druid centre on Mona (60) before Boudica's revolt (60-61) forced him back to win a desperate battle. After a period of consolidation under Turpilianus and Trebellius Maximus, and the loss of the Brigantian client kingdom to Venutius in 69, the Flavian governors resumed the advance: Petillius Cerialis (71-74) defeated the Brigantes and founded the fortress at York, Frontinus (74-77) subdued the Silures and founded Caerleon, and Agricola (77/78-83/84) took Anglesey, built forts across northern England and Scotland and defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius. Domitian's need for troops on the Danube led to the abandonment of the legionary fortress at Inchtuthil and the withdrawal from most of Scotland after 86. The conquest required four legions (three after 86) and some 50,000 troops, the largest garrison of any province relative to size, and its profitability was doubted already by Strabo. Archaeology, from the destruction layers of the Boudican revolt to the Vindolanda tablets and the marching camps of Scotland, has greatly enriched the accounts of Tacitus and Dio.

The revolt of Boudica (60 or 61) was the most dangerous rising in Roman Britain. Its causes, as Tacitus and Dio describe them, were the seizure of the Icenian kingdom after the death of the client king Prasutagus, the flogging of his widow Boudica and the rape of their daughters by the procurator Catus Decianus's men, the confiscation of the estates of the Iceni nobles, the arrogance of the veterans of the colony at Camulodunum who had taken land from the Trinovantes, the burden of the imperial cult temple to Claudius, and the sudden calling in of loans by Roman lenders, including Seneca. While the governor Suetonius Paullinus was attacking Mona with two legions, the Iceni and Trinovantes rose. Camulodunum, without walls, fell after a two-day siege of the temple; a relief force of IX Hispana under Petillius Cerialis was routed, losing its infantry; Catus Decianus fled to Gaul. Paullinus marched to Londinium but decided he could not defend it and left it to its fate; the rebels destroyed Londinium and Verulamium, killing, according to Tacitus, 70,000 citizens and allies with gibbets, fire and crosses, while Dio adds gruesome details of the mutilation of noblewomen. A layer of burnt debris, the "Boudican destruction horizon", has been found at all three cities. Paullinus gathered about 10,000 men of XIV Gemina, part of XX Valeria and auxiliaries (II Augusta failed to come) and defeated the Britons in a battle in a defile, killing 80,000 for a loss of 400 by Tacitus's count. Boudica died, by poison or illness. Reinforcements of 2,000 legionaries, eight cohorts and 1,000 cavalry came from Germany, and Paullinus ravaged the territory of the rebels, leading to famine. The new procurator Julius Classicianus urged leniency, Nero's freedman Polyclitus investigated, and Paullinus was replaced by Petronius Turpilianus, who adopted a conciliatory policy. Nero is said to have considered abandoning Britain. The revolt's date (60 or 61) is debated.
set.debate: Date (60 or 61) and site of the final battle.
